explanations.answer: Do not fear what they fear
explanations.explanation: That's the instruction, baker. The LORD tells Isaiah, “Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread.” (Isaiah 8:12) Panic spreads faster than a yawn in a meeting, so this was a good thing to hear. Isaiah doesn't have to catch it.

explanations.answer: Warn them to fear it more
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse tells Isaiah to turn the fear up. The LORD says, “Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread.” (Isaiah 8:12) The crowd already had plenty of dread without Isaiah adding a second helping.

No running shoes get handed out here, friend. The verse doesn't send Isaiah anywhere. It says, “Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread.” (Isaiah 8:12) The instruction is about where his fear goes, not where his feet go.

Right on target. The LORD says, “The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.” (Isaiah 8:13) Notice the word “only.” That leaves no room for a second name on the list.

I get why you'd pick him. Isaiah just warned that this king would pour into Judah like a flood (Isaiah 8:7-8). But the LORD says, “Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.” (Isaiah 8:13) "He" there is the LORD of Hosts. No king gets in line behind Him.

This verse doesn't mention the king of Judah at all. It says the LORD of Hosts is the One to regard as holy, and then, “Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.” (Isaiah 8:13) That word “only” closes the door on every other name.

Yes, that's what the verse says. The LORD will be a sanctuary, but to both houses of Israel He will be “…a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense…” (Isaiah 8:14). It's one verse with two sides. Good thing you read the second half.

This one is true, friend. The text says the LORD will be a sanctuary, but to both houses of Israel “…a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense…” (Isaiah 8:14). Verse 15 adds that many will stumble over these. It's an easy one to miss when the sanctuary part is the first thing you hear.

explanations.answer: Wait for the LORD and trust Him
explanations.explanation: That's what Isaiah says. “I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him.” (Isaiah 8:17) Waiting isn't flashy. I spent plenty of time waiting myself, so I know it's some of the hardest work there is.

explanations.answer: Look for help from another god
explanations.explanation: Isaiah goes the other direction, baker. He says, “I will wait for the LORD… I will put my trust in Him.” (Isaiah 8:17) A couple of verses later he asks, “…shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19).

Isaiah doesn't go quiet. Right after he says he'll wait and trust, he says, “Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel…” (Isaiah 8:18). That doesn't sound like a man packing up. He says he'll wait for the LORD and put his trust in Him (Isaiah 8:17).

That's what he says. “Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.” (Isaiah 8:18) I think any father would stand a little taller saying that. I know I would.

This one is true, friend. Isaiah says, “Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel…” (Isaiah 8:18). The children are from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. So it's a gift and a sign all at once.

Yes! Isaiah asks, “…shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19) It's a question with its answer built in. The mediums and spiritists are the ones who whisper and mutter, and Isaiah points the people to their God instead.

Elders are a fair guess, since people do go to them for advice. But that's not who Isaiah names in this verse. He asks, “…shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19). The mediums are set against God Himself.

Kings don't come up in this question. Isaiah asks, “…shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19). A king does show up two verses later, but that's a different scene. Here it's the mediums on one side and God on the other.

That's the one. Isaiah asks, “Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19) That question comes right after he talks about mediums and spiritists. The dead are the ones being consulted, and the living are the ones it's for.
My sky is full of constellations, so I get the pull of stars, friend. But Isaiah doesn't mention them here. He asks, “Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19).
Strangers don't show up in this question. Isaiah asks, “Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19). The word that fills the blank is about who is being consulted, and it's the dead.

explanations.answer: Curse their king and their God
explanations.explanation: That's what Isaiah says. I think it's a heavy one. “When they are famished, they will become enraged; and looking upward, they will curse their king and their God.” (Isaiah 8:21) It's a hard picture of people at the end of themselves.

explanations.answer: Cry out to God for mercy
explanations.explanation: I wish the verse went that way, baker. It doesn't. Isaiah says, “…looking upward, they will curse their king and their God.” (Isaiah 8:21) It's a heavy verse, and it's good you saw what it really says.

The king does show up in the verse, but not as a helper. Isaiah says, “…looking upward, they will curse their king and their God.” (Isaiah 8:21) I think this is one of the hard moments in the passage. It helps to see it plainly.

An army would be a lot to see in the dark, friend. But Isaiah says, “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light…” (Isaiah 9:2) What they saw wasn't a fighting force. It was a light.
A storm would make a dark night even darker. Isaiah says the opposite: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light…” (Isaiah 9:2) The blank is a great light.

This one is true, friend. The verse says, “For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor.” (Isaiah 9:4) The oppressor's rod is on that list.

explanations.answer: Burned as fuel for the fire
explanations.explanation: That's right. Isaiah says, “For every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.” (Isaiah 9:5) Nobody is putting those boots in the closet to use again. They're going up in flames.

explanations.answer: Stored up for the next war
explanations.explanation: Nobody's keeping those boots in a closet. Isaiah says they “…will be burned as fuel for the fire.” (Isaiah 9:5) The boots and garments go to the fire, not into storage.

The verse doesn't mention burying anything. Isaiah says every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood “…will be burned as fuel for the fire.” (Isaiah 9:5) The answer is fire, baker, and the fire has a purpose: fuel.

Priests don't appear in this verse at all. Isaiah says, “…the government will be upon His shoulders.” (Isaiah 9:6) That's the child born to us and the son given to us.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end.” (Isaiah 9:7) It keeps growing and there's no end to it. Most things I bake end when somebody grabs the last cookie.
